newsitem.title: USA: U.S. cotton gins at risk under Farm Bill-economist.
newsitem.headline: U.S. cotton gins at risk under Farm Bill-economist.

text.p: Ginners are at greater risk than any other segment of the cotton industry under the 1996 Farm Bill, as cotton loses acreage to other crops, a marketing specialist said.

"The cotton specific operations of gins and smaller warehouses will have financial problems associated with the risk of lower volumes and reduced utilization of capital investments," Carl Anderson, a cotton marketing specialist with Texas A&M University, said.
The 1996 Freedom to Farm Bill capped federal aid to growers and lifted limits on what thay can grow. The bill assures farmers $35 billion through 2002, which will decline in size each year.

Anderson told industry members at the annual Beltwide Cotton Conferences that ginners will be at risk as producers choose among different crops, resulting in lower output and an uncertain economic environment.

He said the smaller gins will encounter financial hardships over the uncertainty of available cotton to gins. Larger gins have the advantage of lower costs per bale, modern equipment and larger volume, he said.

"If economic incentives discourage cotton production in a given area for several years, all or most gins in an area will be forced to close," Anderson warned. "When an area is without feasible ginning capacity, cotton production may cease."
He said the industry must cut the cost of production by about 10 percent.

"If we stay at higher prices then China and the rest of the world will go to 90.00 cent cotton and plant more acres," Anderson told Reuters. "If we lose to foreign producers and synthetics, then we are likely not to recover."
